examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. It is (i) ______ that so many portrait paintings hang in art museums, since the subject matter seems to dictate a status closer to pictures in the family photograph album than to high art. But perhaps it is the artistic skill with which the portraits are painted that (ii) ______ their presence in art museums. Blank (i): A surprising, B understandable, C irrelevant. Blank (ii): D challenges, E justifies, F changes.

solution.operation: Read the clause after "since" in sentence 1: portrait subject matter belongs closer to the family photo album than to high art.
solution.result: Sentence 1 signals that portrait subject matter does not fit the idea of high art.
solution.description: Use the "since" clause as the context clue for the first sentence: it tells you how the writer characterizes the subject matter of portraits.

solution.operation: Translate that mismatch into the sense Blank (i) must carry: the presence of portraits in art museums is odd or unfitting.
solution.result: Blank (i) needs a word meaning odd/unfitting.
solution.description: Convert the clue into a required meaning for the blank before looking at the answer choices, so the choice is tested against a prediction.

solution.operation: Match the Blank (i) choices to "odd or unfitting": surprising, understandable, irrelevant.
solution.result: "surprising" (Choice A) expresses that sense.
solution.description: Compare each first-column choice with the predicted meaning and keep the only one that expresses oddness.

solution.operation: Read sentence 2, which contrasts with sentence 1 and offers a point in favor of portraits: their artistic skill.
solution.result: Sentence 2 supplies a reason why portraits should be in art museums.
solution.description: Track the contrast marked by "But": the second sentence argues for museum placement rather than against it.

solution.operation: Match the Blank (ii) choices to "gives a reason for their presence": challenges, justifies, changes.
solution.result: "justifies" (Choice E) completes that thought.
solution.description: Pick the second-column word that makes artistic skill support the portraits' presence, which is what the sentence's logic requires.

examples.answer: Choice A: surprising; Choice E: justifies

key_reminders: The clause after "since" states the reason the writer has in mind and controls the first blank.
"But" marks a reversal: the second sentence argues for what the first sentence made look odd.
Predict the meaning each blank needs before scanning its column of choices.
common_mistakes: Choosing "understandable" for Blank (i), which contradicts the "since" clause instead of following it.
Choosing "challenges" for Blank (ii), which reverses the pro-portrait direction set up by "But" and "artistic skill".

examples.problem_statement: If x+\frac{1}{yz},\; y+\frac{1}{zx},\; z+\frac{1}{xy} are in A.P., then x, y, z are in:

solution.result: A concrete triple that is itself in A.P. (common difference 1).
solution.description: Instead of manipulating the general expressions, assume x, y, z are in A.P. and pick easy values to test the claim.
Substitute the assumed values into the first given expression to get its numerical value.
Substitute the same values into the second expression to get its numerical value.
Substitute the same values into the third expression to get its numerical value.

solution.result: \frac{7}{6} = \frac{7}{6}, so \frac{7}{6},\frac{7}{3},\frac{7}{2} are in A.P.
solution.description: Compare the two consecutive differences of the three computed values to see whether they form an A.P.

solution.operation: Read the verified implication back: x, y, z in A.P. produced the three expressions in A.P.
solution.result: The condition given in the question is met exactly when x, y, z are in A.P.
solution.description: Conclude from the checked case which progression x, y, z belong to.

key_reminders: Three terms are in A.P. when the difference between consecutive terms is the same.
For a multiple-choice style relation question, assuming convenient values that satisfy one option can confirm it.
common_mistakes: Mis-reading x+1/yz as (x+1)/(yz) instead of x plus the reciprocal of yz, which changes every computed value.

concept.technique_name: odd/even parity rules with value testing

examples.problem_statement: If pq is odd, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) [statement stating a quantity is odd] (B) p + q is even. (C) p - q is odd.

solution.operation: pq \text{ odd} \Rightarrow p \text{ odd and } q \text{ odd}
solution.result: Both p and q must be odd.
solution.description: Apply the parity rule for products: an even factor would force an even product, so a product that is odd forces both factors odd.

solution.operation: Substitute a pair of odd values for p and q into each answer statement.
solution.result: Each statement is evaluated on a case allowed by the constraint.
solution.description: Test the statements with concrete odd values rather than reasoning abstractly, since only odd values are permitted by step 1.

solution.operation: Eliminate every statement that the odd values make false.
solution.result: Only one statement survives the test.
solution.description: Discard any option that fails on a legitimate case, because a "must be true" statement cannot fail on any allowed case.

solution.operation: Identify the surviving statement.
solution.result: p + q is even is the one that remains.
solution.description: Report the only statement not eliminated as the sole correct answer.

key_reminders: A product is odd only when every factor is odd.
"Must be true" means true in every allowed case, so a single counterexample eliminates a statement.
common_mistakes: Treating pq as a two-digit number or as p times q ambiguously, instead of the product whose odd value forces both p and q odd.

concept.sub_category: averages, median and range of combined samples

examples.problem_statement: The earthworms in Sample A have an average length of 2.4 inches, and the earthworms in Sample B have an average length of 3.8 inches. The average length of the earthworms in both samples combined is 3.0 inches. Which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. I. There are more earthworms in Sample A than in Sample B. II. The median length of the earthworms is 3.2 inches. III. The range of lengths of the earthworms is 1.4.

solution.operation: Compare the combined average 3.0 with the two sample averages 2.4 and 3.8.
solution.result: 3.0 is closer to Sample A's 2.4 than to Sample B's 3.8.
solution.description: Locate the overall average between the two sample averages and see which one it sits nearer to.

solution.operation: Read that closeness as a weighting: the combined average is pulled toward the larger sample.
solution.result: Sample A contains more earthworms than Sample B, so statement I must be true.
solution.description: Apply weighted-average reasoning: the sample that pulls the overall average toward its own average is the one with more members.

solution.operation: Ask whether the median can be pinned down from averages alone; note the lengths in Sample A could all equal 2.4 or be spread widely around it.
solution.result: The median is not determined by the given information, so statement II need not be true.
solution.description: Check statement II by observing that many different individual-value distributions produce the same averages, and they do not share one median.

solution.operation: Ask the same of the range; Sample B's lengths could likewise be identical or vary widely while keeping their average.
solution.result: The range is not determined either, so statement III need not be true.
solution.description: Check statement III the same way: without the individual values, the spread of the data set can vary a great deal.

solution.operation: Collect the statements that survived: I only.
solution.result: Only statement I must be true.
solution.description: Report the statements that are forced by the given averages and drop the two that depend on unknown individual values.

key_reminders: A combined average lies nearer the average of the larger group.
Averages alone fix neither the median nor the range; those need the individual values.
common_mistakes: Taking 3.2 as the median because it looks like a plausible middle value between 2.4 and 3.8.
Computing 3.8 - 2.4 = 1.4 and calling it the range, when 1.4 is only the gap between the two sample averages, not between the longest and shortest worms.
